facts.statement: Guanlong was first described in 2006 by Xu Xing and colleagues as a new taxon related to Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: It was first described in 2006 by Xu Xing and colleagues, who found it to represent a new taxon related to Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Guanlong was discovered in the Dzungaria area of China by a joint expedition between the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology and George Washington University.
facts.quote: Guanlong was discovered in the Dzungaria area of China by a joint expedition by scientists from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology and George Washington University

facts.statement: Guanlong is known from two specimens found in the Shishugou Formation, one of which was discovered on top of the other along with three other theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: At present, Guanlong is known from two specimens, one discovered on top of the other, with three other individual theropod dinosaurs, in the Shishugou Formation.

facts.statement: Researchers presume the immature specimen was trampled to death by the adult individual after both died.
facts.quote: It was presumed to have been trampled, after death, by the adult.

facts.statement: The thin, delicate crests of Guanlong likely served as display organs, possibly for mating events.
facts.quote: The crests of both specimens are thin, delicate structures that likely served as display organs, possibly for events like mating.

facts.statement: Unlike later tyrannosaurs, Guanlong possessed three long fingers on its hands.
facts.quote: Unlike later tyrannosaurs, Guanlong had three long fingers on its hands.

facts.statement: Guanlong likely resembled its close relative Dilong and may have possessed a coat of primitive feathers.
facts.quote: Aside from its distinctive crest, it would have resembled its close relative Dilong, and like Dilong may have had a coat of primitive feathers.

facts.statement: Guanlong lived about 160 million years ago during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic, approximately 92 million years before Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Its fossils were found in the Shishugou Formation dating to about 160 million years ago, in the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic period, 92 million years before its well-known relative Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Guanlong lived between 161.5 and 154.8 million years ago during the Oxfordian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Oxfordian to Oxfordian (161.5 to 154.8 million years ago)

facts.statement: The juvenile Guanlong died at 6 years of age while still growing.
facts.quote: The juvenile died at 6, and was still growing.

facts.statement: Juvenile Guanlong exhibited features such as a proportionally shorter snout, larger orbits, larger hands, longer lower legs, and a less expanded pubic bone compared to adults.
facts.quote: In the juvenile, the crest is restricted to the snout, which is proportionally shorter. The orbit is also larger, the hand comparatively larger, the lower leg is longer, the pubic bone has a less expanded end, and other features found in more derived coelurosaurs and tyrannosauroids.

facts.statement: Guanlong possessed a highly pneumatized cranial crest similar to those of Dilophosaurus and Monolophosaurus, likely used for display.
facts.quote: Guanlong possessed a cranial crest, which may have been used for display. It is similar to those of Dilophosaurus and Monolophosaurus, and like those it was highly pneumatized.

facts.statement: A 2013 study classified Guanlong in the family Proceratosauridae alongside Proceratosaurus and Kileskus.
facts.quote: A 2013 study found Guanlong to be in a clade with both Proceratosaurus and Kileskus. Together they formed the family Proceratosauridae

facts.statement: A 2014 study redefined the family Proceratosauridae to include only Guanlong, Proceratosaurus, Kileskus, and Sinotyrannus, excluding Stokesosaurus and Juratyrant.
facts.quote: However, in 2014 another study was published, instead finding Stokesosaurus and Juratyrant outside the family, which only included Guanlong, Proceratosaurus, Kileskus and Sinotyrannus.

facts.statement: A 2024 study placed Dilong and proceratosaurids like Guanlong outside the clade Tyrannosauroidea based on phylogenetic analysis.
facts.quote: In 2024, the describers of Alpkarakush recovered Dilong and proceratosaurids (Proceratosaurus and Guanlong) outside Tyrannosauroidea based on their phylogenetic analysis.

facts.statement: While crests in related genera may have been for species recognition, the gracile crest of Guanlong is more likely used for display purposes.
facts.quote: Structures in Dilophosaurus and Monolophosaurus have also been suggested to be for species recognition, but the more gracile crest of Guanlong is more likely for display purposes.
